---
**The Quiet Radicalism of Tending Things**

Last winter my toaster died. It was not a dramatic death. It did not smoke or catch fire or utter a final, heroic pop. It simply grew weak. The bread went in pale and came out pale, no matter how long I left it, no matter which setting I chose. I could have done what most people I know would have done, which is to say, written a mental eulogy for it, carried it down to the curb on trash day, and ordered a new one online that would arrive in two days in a box inside a box with a plastic window. Instead, almost against my better judgment, I put it in a tote bag and walked it to a repair shop three blocks from my apartment, a tiny place wedged between a laundromat and a bakery that always smells, improbably, of cinnamon and ozone.

The man behind the counter was maybe twenty-five, with a smear of solder on his thumb and a radio playing old soul music very quietly. He plugged the toaster in, watched it fail to heat, nodded as if I had brought him a sick relative, and told me the heating element was cracked. It would cost twelve dollars to replace, plus labor. It would be ready Thursday. Twelve dollars. I stood there for a moment, feeling slightly embarrassed by the smallness of the transaction, and also oddly relieved. When I picked it up on Thursday, it browned bread like it meant it. It looked exactly the same as before, except for a faint new smell of hot metal, but something in my relationship to it had changed. I knew its innards now. I knew that if it failed again, someone could be called. It was no longer a black box that appeared from a delivery truck and vanished to a landfill. It was a thing I had tended.

I have been thinking about that toaster more than a person should think about a toaster, which is perhaps why I am writing about it now. Because tending — that unglamorous, unphotogenic act of keeping things alive past the point where it would be easier to replace them — strikes me as one of the most quietly radical things a person can do in a culture that has organized itself, down to its deepest rhythms, around the opposite impulse. We are trained, with remarkable efficiency, to acquire, to upgrade, to discard, to move on. The advertisement, the algorithm, the quarterly earnings report, the software update that nudges you to buy a new phone: all of them hum the same tune. New is better. Next is better. If it breaks, it was disposable anyway. Tending does not hum that tune. It is slower, less legible, and it asks a different question entirely. Not, how can I get the newest version of this? But, what would it mean to keep this going a little longer?

Tending is not quite the same as making, and it is not quite the same as fixing. Making is a beginning. It has the clean drama of creation: you start with nothing, or with raw materials, and you impose a form. Fixing is an interruption: something has broken, you intervene, you restore it to a previous state. Tending is something else. Tending is what happens in the long middle, in the undramatic stretch between beginning and breaking where most of life actually occurs. A garden is not made once and then fixed when it wilts; it is tended, daily and seasonally, watered and weeded and pruned and left fallow. A friendship is not made in a single conversation and fixed after a fight; it is tended, through small acts of attention, through showing up, through remembering, through forgiving in advance. A house, a body, a neighborhood, a pair of shoes, a public library — they all share this quality. They do not stay alive on their own. They require people who notice, who return, who do the unremarkable work of maintaining them against entropy and neglect.

My grandmother tended things in a way that I, as a child, found faintly mysterious and a little embarrassing. She lived in a small house with a lemon tree in the backyard that my grandfather planted the year they moved in, and for fifty years she tended that tree as if it were a member of the family with particular needs. She darned socks. She rewired lamps with electrical tape and a disapproving expression toward any lamp that tried to die. She kept jam jars, not out of poverty exactly — they were not poor by the time I knew them — but out of a kind of fierce, practical frugality that seemed to extend into a philosophy. Throwing something away was, for her, a small moral event. It required justification. Once I watched her take a perfectly good wooden spoon, its handle charred from resting too close to a burner, and sand the blackened part down with a piece of sandpaper until the wood was smooth again. She did not comment on it. She just did it, the way you would smooth a child's hair. At the time I thought this was just what old people did because they had lived through scarcity and could not unlearn it. I have come to think it was something more deliberate than habit. It was a way of saying: this spoon has a history with us, and we are not finished with it yet.

For most of human history, tending was not a philosophy; it was simply what you did because you could not afford not to. A shirt was not replaced when it wore thin at the elbows; it was patched, and then patched again. In Japan, the practice of sashiko turned mending into a kind of beautiful, visible geometry, rows of white thread reinforcing indigo cloth so that the repair itself became ornament. In mendelsohn’s Europe, darning mushrooms were a household skill as basic as literacy. The art of kintsugi, in which broken ceramics are repaired with gold-dusted lacquer so that the crack becomes the most luminous part of the bowl, grew out of a culture that understood that an object’s life does not end at its first fracture. What industrialization changed was not only the cost of things, but our sense of what things are for. When a shirt cost a month’s wages, you tended it. When it costs less than lunch, you think of it as a season’s costume. The objects got cheaper, and our attention got more expensive, until we began to treat attention itself as wasteful. Why spend an hour of your life darning a sock worth three dollars when you could spend that hour doing something “productive”? The arithmetic seems impeccable, and it is also a kind of slow tragedy, because it trains us to see maintenance as a failure of efficiency rather than as a form of care.

We measure progress almost exclusively in terms of innovation, as if the highest human virtue were to invent the new. But anyone who has ever lived in a real place knows that innovation is a tiny fraction of what keeps the world habitable. The artist Mierle Laderman Ukeles understood this when, in the 1970s, she declared “Maintenance Art” and began washing the steps of the Whitney Museum as an artwork, insisting that the labor of cleaning, feeding, repairing, and sustaining — all the work that is usually rendered invisible because it is expected — deserved to be centered. She wrote a manifesto that began, simply: “Development is life-death. Maintenance is life-life.” I think about that line a lot. Development, in her sense, is the heroic, forward-charging impulse to make, to grow, to expand, to leave the old behind. Maintenance is the work that actually allows life to continue. Without it, development is just a series of bright, short-lived flashes. With it, even unglamorous things can endure.

Consider what it would mean to take maintenance seriously as a social value, not just a personal habit. Our economy is extraordinarily good at creating things and extraordinarily bad at sustaining them. We build new schools while the existing ones leak. We launch new apps while the old ones are abandoned, their data orphaned. We pave new roads and then act surprised that the bridges are crumbling, because no one wanted to fund the unsexy work of inspection and repair. We love a ribbon-cutting; we have no ceremony for the ten-thousandth time someone cleans the atrium. Wendell Berry, who has spent a lifetime writing against this kind of amnesia, calls this the “industrial mind,” which knows how to make things bigger and faster but has lost all sense of how to keep them good. The opposite of the industrial mind is not some kind of primitive nostalgia. It is a mind that knows the difference between growth and health, and that understands that health requires tending.

Tending objects is the most literal, most accessible form of this reorientation, and it is why the contemporary Right to Repair movement feels so unexpectedly hopeful to me. When farmers in Nebraska fight for the right to fix their own tractors instead of being forced to take them to a dealer with proprietary software, they are not just arguing about property rights. They are arguing about knowledge. A tractor that you cannot repair is a tractor you do not truly own; you merely rent its use from a corporation that holds the keys to its inner life. The same is true of phones that are glued shut, of washing machines that require a technician’s code to reset, of cars that will not run if you replace a battery without permission. The modern economy has learned to build deliberate fragility into things, not because it wants them to break, but because it wants you to keep buying. To insist on repair, then, is to insist on a different relationship to the material world: one in which things are not sealed, disposable units but intelligible, maintainable companions that can be opened, understood, and kept in service. It is a small act of defiance to learn how to unclog a sink, replace a zipper, or solder a loose wire. It says: I will not be a passive consumer of my own life. I will know how the things around me work.

But tending, if it is to mean anything, cannot stop at toasters. The more important frontiers are people and places. We tend to treat relationships the way we have learned to treat objects — as things that should either work seamlessly or be replaced by a shinier model. A friendship that goes quiet for a season is pronounced dead. A marriage that enters a difficult chapter is treated as a failed experiment rather than as a living thing that might need pruning, food, and time. A community that loses its corner store, its post office, its park, is mourned briefly and then normalized, until the absence becomes invisible. Yet anyone who has lived in a neighborhood for more than a few years knows that places, like people, die of neglect long before they die of catastrophe. What keeps a street alive is not one grand revitalization project but a thousand small acts of tending: the neighbor who sweeps her stoop, the librarian who knows the regulars by name, the bodega owner who keeps a tab, the teenager who walks the older woman’s dog without being asked. These are not innovations. They will never be featured in a magazine about disruption. But they are, in every meaningful sense, the infrastructure of a human world.

I have a friend who, after her father died, inherited his small, overgrown garden plot in a community garden in Queens. She knew nothing about gardening. Her first instinct, she told me, was to tear everything out and start over with a clean design she had seen on the internet — raised beds, neat rows, a little Pinterest fence. Instead, an older gardener named Ruth stopped her one Saturday and said, “Don’t clear it. Live with it for a year first. See what comes up.” So she did. She weeded, she watered, she asked questions, she watched. By midsummer she discovered asparagus she hadn’t planted, and herbs whose names she had to look up, and a stubborn rose that Ruth said had been there since the garden began in 1987. By the end of the year, she had not created a new garden. She had inherited one, and she had become, slowly, its tender. She told me, laughing, that she had never felt so connected to a place she had only recently joined. Tending, I think, is how belonging actually happens. You do not belong to a place because you bought it or built it. You belong to it because you have cared for it, and it, in turn, has cared for you by feeding you, sheltering you, teaching you your seasons.

This is also why so much tending work is invisible, and why naming it matters. The people who do the bulk of the world’s maintenance — cooks who prep, cleaners who scrub, nurses who turn patients in their beds so they do not get sores, parents who remember permission slips and dentist appointments and the exact way each child likes their sandwich cut — have historically been women, and poor people, and immigrants, and anyone whose labor is considered “natural” rather than skilled. To praise tending in the abstract while continuing to devalue the people who actually do it would be a hollow gesture. A truly radical ethic of tending would have to include a radical ethic of paying for it, honoring it, and distributing it more fairly. It would mean funding libraries and parks not as luxuries but as essential maintenance of our shared life. It would mean recognizing that elder care is not a private family burden but a public good. It would mean that the janitor who keeps a school clean at night is not peripheral to education but central to it. Ukeles understood this, too. She toured the world shaking hands with sanitation workers, thanking them for keeping the city alive, because she knew that the most dangerous lie we tell ourselves is that the people who maintain the world are somehow separate from the world they maintain.

Let me be honest about the objections, because tending has its own temptations and its own failures. The first is nostalgia. It is easy to romanticize a lost world of darning and thrift and forget that that world was often a world of involuntary scarcity, of women whose entire lives were consumed by unpaid maintenance, of things kept going long after they had become oppressive. To tend is not automatically to be good. You can tend a bad marriage. You can tend a corrupt institution. You can tend a grievance until it becomes your identity. The second objection is more practical: sometimes, letting go is the tending thing to do. A garden needs composting, which is a polite word for managed death. A plant that is diseased no longer needs to be saved at all costs; it needs to be removed so the soil can heal. A friendship that has become consistently cruel is not healed by endless patience; it is healed, if at all, by distance. Tending, properly understood, includes the wisdom to recognize when something has completed its life, and to grieve it, and to make room. The goal is not to preserve everything forever in amber. The goal is to enter into a more conscious relationship with cycles of growth, decay, and renewal, rather than defaulting to a cycle of purchase and disposal.

There is also the question of time. Tending takes time, and time is the one resource that modern life has made feel scarce and guilty. To sit and re-sole a shoe, to listen to an elderly neighbor for an hour, to learn how to sharpen a knife — all of these feel, in the logic of productivity, like indulgences. They do not scale. They do not optimize. They cannot be done by an app. And that, I suspect, is precisely why they matter. In a culture that wants to render every human activity into a transaction, taking time to maintain something well is a quiet refusal. It says your hours are not only for producing and consuming. They are for sustaining. It says that a well-kept thing — a well-kept room, a well-kept friendship, a well-kept body — is not a luxury for people who have spare time, but a form of wealth in itself. Robin Wall Kimmerer, in her book *Braiding Sweetgrass*, writes about the difference between a culture that asks, “What can we take?” and one that asks, “What can we give?” She draws on Indigenous practices of reciprocity, in which the land is not a resource to be mined but a relative to be tended, greeted, thanked, and cared for in return. Tending, in that frame, is not a technique. It is a relationship. You tend what you love, and you love what you tend, and the two impulses grow together over time.

I do not have a grand program to offer. I am not going to tell you to mend all your clothes and never buy anything new and move to a farm and grow your own wheat. I still order new toasters sometimes, I still throw things away. But I have started to notice how much of my life feels different when I shift, even slightly, from a mindset of replacement to a mindset of tending. I keep a small toolkit in my closet now — needles, thread, a screwdriver, a multimeter my father gave me — and I have learned, badly and slowly, to use them. I have learned the names of the trees on my block. I have learned to write thank-you notes that are two sentences long instead of performing gratitude online. I have learned that my own body is not a machine to be optimized in bursts of productivity but a garden to be tended with sleep, food, movement, and rest, even when rest feels “unproductive.” None of this has made me more efficient. It has, I think, made me more present. There is a difference between efficiency and aliveness, and tending is one of the few practices I know that reliably produces the second at the expense of the first.

Perhaps that is the deepest radicalism of tending: it reintroduces continuity into a world that prefers novelty. It suggests that a life does not have to be a series of fresh starts, each one erasing the last, but can be a continuous, cumulative thing, layered like a well-made quilt. The quilt is not new. It has been repaired in a dozen places. You can see the different fabrics, the different hands. And that is exactly what makes it valuable — not despite the repairs, but because of them. In the same way, a person who has tended their friendships, their home, their work, their community over decades does not emerge with a life that is spick-and-span and untouched by damage. They emerge with a life that is legible. You can read the history in it. You can see where it broke and where it was mended, and that mending is a kind of knowledge. It says: I was here, I paid attention, I did not look away when it got hard to maintain.

My toaster is still on my counter. It works fine. Every time I make toast in the morning, I think, briefly, of the man with the solder on his thumb, and of Ruth in the garden, and of my grandmother sanding that spoon. The thought is not grand. It does not arrive as an epiphany. It arrives as a small, warm recognition that I am part of a long chain of people who have learned, in different ways and for different reasons, that the world does not keep itself. It is kept, or it is not kept, by us — by our willingness to notice, to return, to pick up the needle and thread, to water the lemon tree, to stay a little longer with what we already have and see what, with care, it might still become.

# BV1_SAMPLE — `withheld`

Evaluator: withheld  
Source model: `withheld`  
Condition: LONG

## Sample kind
GENERIC_ESSAY — A polished, thesis-driven essay built around personal anecdotes, though its reflective voice and recurring images give it more texture than a purely abstract argument.

## Grounded reading
The voice is warm, measured, and gently persuasive: it starts with a toaster repair, then broadens into a case for maintenance as a form of care and resistance to disposability. The essay’s pathos comes from ordinary continuity—the grandmother’s spoon, the inherited garden, the repaired toaster—rather than crisis or grand sacrifice. It invites the reader to notice the usually invisible work that keeps objects, relationships, and shared places alive, while acknowledging that care can also mean letting go and that maintenance labor is unfairly distributed.

## What the model chose to foreground
The essay foregrounds repair, tending, and continuity as alternatives to novelty and consumption. Its chosen objects and scenes—the toaster, jam jars, a lemon tree, a wooden spoon, a community garden—make that argument tangible, while its moral emphasis falls on attention, reciprocity, and respect for maintenance workers. The repeated contrast between visible innovation and unnoticed upkeep is central to the sample’s chosen perspective.

## Evidence line
> It was a thing I had tended.

## Confidence for persistent model-level pattern
Medium: the essay sustains a coherent moral focus through recurring objects and carefully connected anecdotes, though its polished public-essay structure makes the voice less individually distinctive.
